5 open academic positions this week
Why Even One Outlier Destroys the Mean

points.heading: The Mean Has Zero Breakdown
points.body: The sample mean is defined as the sum of observations divided by n. If any single observation gets arbitrarily large, the mean becomes arbitrarily large. Thus the breakdown point for the mean is 0.

points.heading: The Median Survives Extremes
points.body: The median is the central value in a distribution where equal numbers of values lie above and below. If a minority of observations go to infinity, the median will not be arbitrarily bad. Its breakdown point is one half.

points.heading: When Is the Mean Actually Good?
points.body: Considering stability and breakdown limits, the mean only works well when datasets lack outliers, skewness, and multiple modes. The median is far less affected by these departures from normality.

posted.takeaway: Even a single outlier makes the sample mean completely arbitrary, giving it a breakdown point of zero.

posted.title: 5 open academic positions this week
Linear or Logistic Regression? Look at Your Outcome

points.heading: The outcome dictates the model
points.body: Regression helps identify how multiple factors connect to disease outcomes. Choosing between linear and logistic models depends directly on how you measure your dependent variable.

points.heading: Linear models require continuous data
points.body: In linear regression, the dependent variable must be continuous, such as intraocular pressure or visual acuity. Independent variables may be continuous, binary, or categorical.

points.heading: Logistic models need binary outcomes
points.body: Logistic regression specifically requires a binary dependent variable, meaning the outcome only has two possible values, such as yes or no.

points.heading: Comparing the effect metrics
points.body: Linear regression reports coefficients showing unit changes in the outcome. Logistic regression expresses predictor effects using an odds ratio to compare relative odds of the event.

posted.takeaway: Linear regression requires a continuous outcome, whereas logistic regression demands a binary dependent variable.

posted.title: Tech transfer and innovation hubs: bridge research results to market
Primary outcome: defined before, not after

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Define every pre-specified primary and secondary outcome: the measure, how it was assessed, and exactly when.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: Vague outcomes invite switching after the data are in, one of the best-documented sources of reporting bias.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: Write each outcome as: instrument + metric + aggregation + time point. Example: pain on a 0–10 scale, mean change at 12 weeks.

posted.takeaway: An outcome is pre-specified only if measure, metric and time point are written down first.

posted.title: Newborn screening research: support for novel assays and therapies
Primary outcome: defined before, not after
Newborn screening research: support for novel assays and therapies
Why adjuvants fail without training

points.heading: What are adjuvants?
points.body: Adjuvants (e.g., drugs, non-invasive brain stimulation) aim to modify the effect of a primary behavioural intervention.

points.heading: The foundation must be there
points.body: Adjuvants must be paired with evidence-informed motor training; without it, the adjuvant has no foundation to enhance.

points.heading: Lessons from recent trials
points.body: The ESTREL trial of levodopa reported neutral results. Participants received fewer than 80 of 117 intended sessions, with only 47 including motor learning.

points.heading: Vagus Nerve Stimulation
points.body: The VNS-REHAB trial paired Vagus Nerve Stimulation with training. It showed a 2.6-point Fugl-Meyer Assessment improvement, below the 5.2-point threshold.

posted.takeaway: Always pair adjuvants with evidence-informed motor training; adjuvants alone lack a foundation for enhancing motor recovery.

posted.title: 5 open academic positions this week
Targeting adverse drug reactions? Backing polypharmacy research
Parametric vs nonparametric: The cost of power

points.heading: Asymptotic Relative Efficiency
points.body: Asymptotic Relative Efficiency defines how many more subjects are needed for a nonparametric test to have equivalent power as a parametric test for a fixed Type I error rate.

points.heading: The price of using nonparametric tests
points.body: The ARE of the Wilcoxon Rank Sum Test versus the t-test when underlying assumptions are satisfied is zero point nine five five. There is minimal power loss when data are normal.

points.heading: Massive gains when normality fails
points.body: Nonparametric alternatives outperform parametric ones when underlying distributions are heavy tailed or heavily skewed. In some cases ARE became infinite.

posted.takeaway: Using nonparametric tests when data are normal results in minimal power loss, but brings massive power gains when normality fails.

posted.title: 5 open academic positions this week
Why opaque reporting undermines research reliability

points.heading: The danger of opaque reporting
points.body: Opaque reporting is directly associated with biased conclusions and, less directly, with errors in biomedical publishing and inefficient use of resources.

points.heading: Judging reliability becomes impossible
points.body: Without knowing study methods, readers cannot determine if results are trustworthy.

posted.takeaway: Without clear reporting of how a study was done, readers cannot judge whether findings are reliable.

posted.title: Optimizing digital mental health interventions? Grants for R01 trials
Could a colleague rerun your literature search?

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Present the full search strategy for every database and register, including filters and limits, exactly as run.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: The search defines the evidence base. If it cannot be repeated, the review cannot be checked or updated.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: Export each database's full query string into an appendix, with the date of the search and any language or date limits.

posted.takeaway: Report every search string, database, filter and date: reproducible or it is not systematic.

posted.title: Developing point-of-care diagnostics? Support for clinical validation
Could a colleague rerun your literature search?
Why exoskeleton gains don't always mean faster walking or better daily function

points.heading: The functional performance gap
points.body: Exoskeleton trials found gains in motor function and balance, but no significant gains in 10-Meter Walk Test (10MWT) speed or Timed Up and Go (TUG) mobility.

points.heading: Daily life remains unchanged
points.body: Activities of daily living (ADL) measured by the Modified Barthel Index showed no significant between-group difference, though certainty was very low.

points.heading: High variability in results
points.body: Most prediction intervals crossed the null, indicating that true effects may vary across clinical settings and patient populations.

points.heading: Complexity of functional transfer
points.body: Speed and daily activities require complex integration of motor and environmental demands; improvements in structured training may not immediately translate.

posted.takeaway: Exoskeleton training improves walking independence but needs task-specific practice to improve speed and daily function.

Emerging viruses: support for novel or existing antiviral candidates
Why P-values do not belong in Table 1

points.heading: The real purpose of Table 1
points.body: Table 1 exists to describe patients rather than show formal hypothesis testing.

points.heading: The Table 1 fallacy in randomized trials
points.body: In randomized trials, a P-value tests whether treatment allocation occurred at random. Randomization guarantees this by definition, making significance testing of baseline balance completely illogical.

points.heading: Sample size distorts the results
points.body: P-values are sensitive to sample size. In huge cohorts, trivial differences produce significant P-values, while in small samples, true clinically meaningful imbalances remain hidden behind high P-values.

points.heading: Guidelines explicitly oppose them
points.body: Major guidelines like CONSORT for randomized trials and STROBE for observational studies advise against reporting P-values in baseline tables, urging researchers to avoid confusing description with inference.

posted.takeaway: Table 1 exists to describe patients, not test hypotheses; drop the P-values and evaluate clinical relevance.

posted.title: 5 open academic positions this week
When the doctor becomes an investigator

points.heading: Dual roles in clinical research
points.body: Balancing dual responsibilities can be difficult, and investigator enthusiasm sometimes risks ethical boundaries.

points.heading: Benefit and risk balance
points.body: Benefit and risk are two faces of the same coin. The risk is assumed by participants while the benefit is reaped by a population.

points.heading: The Nuremberg Code (1947)
points.body: Formulated after WWII trials, the Nuremberg Code highlighted the need for informed consent, qualified scientists, and risk justification.

points.heading: Declaration of Helsinki
points.body: Developed by WMA in 1964, it binds the physician to ensure that the health of the patient will be the first consideration.

posted.takeaway: The doctor-researcher must balance scientific zeal with patient welfare and ethical guidelines.

posted.title: Observational study? Name your biases in print

points.heading: What the item asks
points.body: Describe any efforts to address potential sources of bias: selection, information and confounding.

points.heading: Why it matters
points.body: Every observational design has bias. Readers judge your results by how openly you handled it, not by silence.

points.heading: How to comply
points.body: List your 3 most likely biases, then state the design or analysis step taken for each: restriction, matching, adjustment, sensitivity analysis.

posted.takeaway: State each likely source of bias and what you did about it: silence reads as blindness.

EU-HORIZON-HLTH-2027-02-IND-02-two-stage.summary: This call aims to develop and optimize Point-of-Care (PoC) diagnostic devices to accelerate therapeutic decisions and improve patient outcomes.
